scope_note: A sourced comparison of the tools and algorithms that turn a full-precision model checkpoint into a quantized one -- method, calibration cost, bit-width flexibility, accuracy retention, and hardware kernel support for the output. Deliberately scoped around Runtimes' quant-specialist category, which covers serving a quantized model rather than producing one. This project runs no accuracy benchmarks of its own; quality-retention claims are attributed and marked accordingly.
method_note: Every claim is checked against the vendor's own documentation or source repository before publication, then adversarially audited in a second pass that actively tries to refute each field rather than confirm it, followed by a dedicated facet-recheck pass verifying every facet against the row's own (possibly-corrected) text. Accuracy/quality figures are mostly vendor-reported and marked verification: vendor-claim unless independently confirmed.

systems.name: AutoAWQ
systems.method: Activation-aware Weight Quantization (AWQ): calibrates on a small activation dataset to identify the small fraction of weight channels most affected by activation outliers, protects those channels with a per-channel scaling factor, then rounds the (now-easier-to-quantize) weights to 4-bit — a lighter-weight search than GPTQ's per-layer Hessian reconstruction.
systems.availability: Python library only, pip-installable (no CLI) — archived, no longer maintained
systems.best_for: Historical reference only — reading or loading legacy AWQ checkpoints already produced with it; new projects should not start here.
systems.watch: The repository was archived by its maintainer on 2025-05-11. The README states outright: "AutoAWQ is officially deprecated and will no longer be maintained," and points users to llm-compressor's AWQ modifier (or MLX-LM for Mac) instead.
systems.standout: Was the reference pip-installable implementation that popularized AWQ separately from the original mit-han-lab research repo; its GEMM/GEMV kernel-naming split is still the convention other AWQ-producing tools follow.
systems.calibration: Needed a calibration dataset (activation statistics) to compute per-channel protection scales; lighter-weight than GPTQ's per-layer Hessian reconstruction, which was part of why it was historically faster to run.
systems.bit_widths: 4-bit (W4A16), with separate GEMM and GEMV kernel variants
systems.kernel_support: Its own GEMM and GEMV CUDA kernels; AWQ checkpoints it produced remain loadable by vLLM, TGI, and other runtimes' own AWQ kernels.
systems.output_format: AWQ safetensors checkpoint; also supported export to GGUF and ExLlamaV2
systems.adoption: Was the default AWQ path for Hugging Face models through 2023-2024; adoption has since moved to llm-compressor's AWQ modifier and to GPTQModel.
systems.verification_note: Archived status, deprecation notice, license, and method confirmed directly from the GitHub README (repository archived by its maintainer on 2025-05-11).

systems.name: AutoRound
systems.method: Weight rounding optimization via sign-gradient descent (SignSGD): introduces trainable per-tensor rounding-value and clipping-range parameters and optimizes them block-by-block against calibration data to minimize block-wise output reconstruction error, rather than a closed-form Hessian solve (GPTQ) or a single calibrated-scale search (AWQ).
systems.availability: Python library / CLI
systems.best_for: Teams chasing the best accuracy retention at very low bit-widths (2-3 bit) who can afford a calibration/optimization pass, especially since it exports to AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, and GGUF rather than locking you into a proprietary loader.
systems.watch: The default settings trade speed for accuracy: the highest-accuracy configuration runs roughly 4-5x slower than the default per the README, so budget calibration time accordingly if chasing the vendor's published low-bit numbers.
systems.standout: Exports to more downstream formats (AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GGUF, LLM-Compressor) than any single-format competitor here, so the accuracy gains carry over to whichever serving stack you already use.
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration dataset (defaults to NeelNanda/pile-10k, 128 samples at 2048 tokens by default, 512 samples for the highest-accuracy mode). A 7B model quantizes in roughly 10 minutes on a single GPU in the default mode; a fast pure-RTN mode is available, and the highest-accuracy mode runs about 4-5x slower than default.
systems.bit_widths: 2, 3, 4, and 8-bit weight quantization (W2A16 through W8A16), plus FP8 and experimental MXFP4/NVFP4
systems.accuracy_note: Intel reports "leading results" at 2-4 bit weight-only quantization versus other PTQ methods, and roughly 97.9% accuracy retention for DeepSeek-R1 at INT2-mixed precision; these are the vendor's own published benchmark numbers, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Ships its own inference kernel library, AutoRound Kernel (ARK), for Intel CPU (Xeon Scalable) and XPU (Arc B-series) — used automatically by default for any AutoRound-quantized model on those platforms, with no extra configuration, including MoE grouped-GEMM and SageAttention kernels. For other backends it reuses the destination format's kernels: AutoGPTQ/AutoAWQ (Marlin, ExLlamaV2, Triton) on CUDA, or llama.cpp on GGUF.
systems.output_format: Native AutoRound format, plus export to AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GGUF, and llm-compressor / compressed-tensors
systems.adoption: Intel-maintained; integrated into Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, and llm-compressor (the vLLM project has its own RFC to add AutoRound support).
systems.verification_note: License, algorithm, calibration defaults, and export formats confirmed from the GitHub README (recent activity through July 2026); the specific accuracy-retention percentages are Intel's own published benchmark numbers (vendor-claim).

systems.name: GPTQModel
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 for the core toolkit; the optional Swordfish CUDA kernel (vendored under gptqmodel_ext/swordfish/, used for newer NVIDIA architectures such as Blackwell) is separately licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later and is compiled/linked only at runtime via JIT when that kernel path is selected — this mixed licensing is why GitHub's own detector reports the repo as "Other" rather than a clean Apache-2.0.
systems.method: Primarily implements GPTQ: layer-wise, calibration-based weight rounding that uses a Hessian approximation of the local loss surface to correct quantization error from already-quantized weights when rounding the rest of a layer, driven by forward passes over a calibration set. The same toolkit also implements AWQ (activation-aware channel scaling), several newer algorithms (EXL3, QQQ, GPTAQ, ParoQuant, FOEM), and calibration-free weight-only export paths (GGUF, FP8) — the calibration approach depends on which method you select. For mixture-of-experts models, dedicated controls (ExpertsRoutingOverride/ExpertsRoutingBypass, plus a FailSafe fallback) let you quantize or skip individual routed experts rather than only offering one setting for the whole model.
systems.availability: Python library / CLI
systems.best_for: Teams who want one toolkit covering many quantization formats (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, FP8, EXL3) and the widest hardware kernel matrix (CUDA, ROCm, XPU, Ascend NPU, Apple/Intel/AMD CPU) rather than committing to a single vendor's format.
systems.watch: Calibration-based methods in this toolkit (GPTQ, AWQ, EXL3, GPTAQ) still need a calibration dataset and a per-layer Hessian-style solve, the same compute-heavy step that makes base GPTQ take hours on the largest models, so speed gains are relative to AutoGPTQ rather than calibration-free. Kernel support (Marlin, BitBLAS, Exllama, Triton) varies by exported format and hardware backend, so the format you pick has to match your serving target. The project overall is Apache-2.0, but the optional Swordfish kernel (used on the newest NVIDIA architectures, e.g. Blackwell) is vendored under a separate AGPL-3.0-or-later license and JIT-compiled at first use — teams with copyleft-sensitive deployments should confirm which kernel path they end up linking before shipping.
systems.standout: Per the project's own history it has "fully supplanted AutoGPTQ and AutoAWQ" for Hugging Face Transformers/Optimum/PEFT integration, and covers more export formats (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, FP8, EXL3, QQQ) and hardware backends than any single-format competitor in this list.
systems.calibration: Calibration-based methods (GPTQ, AWQ, EXL3, GPTAQ) need a calibration dataset and a per-layer Hessian-based solve; the GGUF and FP8 weight-only export paths skip calibration entirely.
systems.bit_widths: 2-bit and 3-bit (GPTQ), 4-bit and 8-bit (primary targets across methods), plus variable average bits-per-weight via EXL3
systems.kernel_support: Marlin, Exllama V2/V3, Triton, BitBLAS, and per-format kernels (GEMM/GEMV for AWQ) across NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Intel XPU, Huawei Ascend NPU, and Apple/Intel/AMD CPU.
systems.output_format: GPTQ/Marlin/BitBLAS safetensors, GGUF, FP8, EXL3, QQQ, and other per-method checkpoint formats
systems.adoption: Merged into Hugging Face Transformers, Optimum, and PEFT as the maintained successor to AutoGPTQ; per the project's own history it has "fully supplanted AutoGPTQ and AutoAWQ" for that integration.
systems.verification_note: License confirmed from the GitHub LICENSE file (Apache-2.0) for the core toolkit; cross-checked against GitHub's own license detector, which flags the repo as mixed ("Other") because an optional Swordfish kernel component (gptqmodel_ext/swordfish/LICENSE) is separately licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later, JIT-compiled at runtime. Algorithm list, hardware/kernel matrix, and release history (v7.4.0, August 4 2026) confirmed directly from the GitHub README and release history. The AutoGPTQ-supplanted / actively-maintained-backend claim is independently corroborated by Hugging Face's own transformers documentation (huggingface.co/docs/transformers/quantization/gptq), not just the project's self-description. No unverified accuracy figures were included.

systems.name: HQQ (Half-Quadratic Quantization)
systems.method: Calibration-free weight-only quantization: solves a robust, sparsity-promoting (Lp, p<1 norm) optimization for each group's scale and zero-point directly from the weight statistics via half-quadratic splitting, with no forward passes over a calibration dataset required.
systems.availability: Python library
systems.best_for: Fast turnaround quantization when you don't have (or don't want to curate) a calibration set, or need to quantize very large models quickly.
systems.watch: No calibration step means no data-driven outlier protection either — at the lowest bit-widths (2-bit and below) the project's own docs point to a companion low-rank adapter (HQQ+) or fine-tuning to recover the quality that calibrated methods like GPTQ/AWQ get from calibration data.
systems.standout: Calibration-free: quantizes in minutes rather than the hours calibration-based methods like GPTQ can take on the largest models, because there is no calibration forward pass to run at all.
systems.calibration: Calibration-free by design — no dataset or forward passes needed. The project's own blog reports quantizing Llama-2-70B in under 5 minutes (vendor-claim).
systems.accuracy_note: The project's own blog states HQQ's 4-bit quantization outperforms bitsandbytes (BNB) in both perplexity and VRAM usage, and quantizes Llama-2-70B in under 5 minutes versus GPTQ's much longer run time — these are the team's own reported comparisons, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Native PyTorch backend by default; optional ATEN/CUDA and Triton (GemLite) backends, TorchAO integration, and vLLM support.
systems.output_format: Safetensors / HQQ's own quantized tensor representation
systems.adoption: Integrated into Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and TorchAO; developed by Mobius Labs (the repository is now hosted under the dropbox GitHub org, with the mobiusml URL redirecting to it).
systems.verification_note: License, calibration-free method, and bit-width support confirmed from the GitHub README; the specific speed and accuracy-vs-bitsandbytes comparisons are the team's own blog claims (vendor-claim).

systems.name: QTIP
systems.method: Trellis Coded Quantization (TCQ) with incoherence processing: first applies a randomized orthogonal transform (incoherence processing, inherited from the QuIP# lineage) to make weight matrices approximately i.i.d. Gaussian, then quantizes with a stateful trellis/bitshift-code structure that decouples codebook size from bitrate, aiming for near-optimal rate-distortion at very low bit-widths without the codebook-size blowup of plain vector quantization.
systems.availability: Python library / research code with install instructions, example scripts, and pre-quantized Hugging Face checkpoints
systems.best_for: Research and experimentation with state-of-the-art sub-4-bit accuracy/speed tradeoffs, when GPL-3.0 licensing is acceptable for the use case.
systems.watch: Licensed GPL-3.0, not the permissive Apache/MIT terms of most tools in this category — a real copyleft obligation to check before embedding it in a closed-source product. The repo now points to newer follow-up work (YAQA) as an improvement, and there has been no commit activity since mid-2025.
systems.standout: Trellis-coded (stateful bitshift-trellis) quantization separates codebook size from bitrate, which is what lets it hit near-optimal distortion at 2-4 bits without the large codebooks vector-quantization methods like QuIP#/VPTQ otherwise need.
systems.calibration: Needs calibration/Hessian data, inherited from the QuIP# codebase it builds on; the repo does not state a specific quantization wall-clock time in its README.
systems.bit_widths: 2, 3, and 4-bit, with matrix-vector multiplication kernels shipped for each
systems.accuracy_note: The QTIP paper reports better perplexity than AQLM and QuIP# at matched 2-4 bit rates on standard benchmarks; these are the authors' own NeurIPS 2024 paper numbers, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Custom CUDA matrix-vector multiplication kernels for 2/3/4-bit, tested on RTX 6000 Ada; not integrated into mainstream serving engines' kernel libraries the way GPTQ/AWQ are.
systems.output_format: Custom trellis-coded checkpoint (HYB code configuration), distributed as Hugging Face-compatible model repos
systems.adoption: Cornell RelaxML research group (QuIP#/QTIP lineage); pre-quantized Llama 2/3.1 checkpoints published on Hugging Face; presented at NeurIPS 2024.
systems.verification_note: License (GPL-3.0), method, and bit-widths confirmed from the GitHub README; commit history shows no activity since June 2025. The perplexity comparisons against AQLM/QuIP# are the authors' own NeurIPS 2024 paper numbers (vendor-claim).

systems.name: SmoothQuant
systems.method: Activation-aware weight-activation smoothing: computes a per-channel smoothing factor offline from calibration activation statistics that mathematically migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights, so both the (now-smoothed) weights and activations can be quantized to simple, symmetric INT8 — enabling full W8A8 (weights AND activations quantized), not just weight-only compression.
systems.availability: Python library (research repo); the algorithm is also reimplemented as a modifier inside vLLM's llm-compressor
systems.best_for: The reference case for accurately quantizing both weights and activations to INT8 to get real compute speedup on int8 GEMM hardware, not just memory savings.
systems.watch: The reference repo has had no commits since mid-2024. More importantly, its own README has always told users not to use this PyTorch implementation for real speedup: "For measured speedup, we recommend using the NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM implementation... we recommend using the FasterTransformer implementation" for multi-GPU setups -- this repo is a correctness/algorithm reference, not the fast path even back when it was actively maintained. Separately, for a still-maintained way to apply the algorithm itself today, vLLM's llm-compressor ships a SmoothQuant modifier.
systems.standout: The original activation-smoothing technique that made W8A8 (weight+activation) quantization practical for LLMs without retraining — most later weight+activation tools trace back to this idea.
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration dataset — 512 random sentences from the Pile validation set by default — used only to compute per-channel activation scales (not a full optimization loop like GPTQ), so it is a comparatively cheap calibration pass. Pre-computed scales ship for several model families.
systems.bit_widths: W8A8 (8-bit weights AND 8-bit activations)
systems.accuracy_note: The paper reports "negligible loss in accuracy" for W8A8 versus FP16 baselines across OPT-175B, BLOOM-176B, GLM-130B, and MT-NLG 530B; these are the original ICML 2023 paper's own numbers, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Its own CUTLASS INT8 GEMM kernels (via torch-int) on NVIDIA CUDA; the algorithm has also been adopted into FasterTransformer, ONNX Runtime, TensorRT-LLM, and AMD's Composable Kernel (MI300X) by other projects.
systems.output_format: PyTorch checkpoint with INT8 linear layers via save_pretrained() (reference repo's examples/export_int8_model.py) -- but that export path targets OPT models only; the later-added architectures (Llama, Falcon, Mistral, Mixtral) are wired through the repo's fake_quant.py simulation for perplexity evaluation, with no equivalent script producing a deployable INT8 checkpoint for them. Downstream integrations (TensorRT-LLM, ONNX Runtime) use their own serialized formats.
systems.adoption: Adopted into Microsoft ONNX Runtime, Amazon SageMaker, NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, and Intel Neural Compressor per the repo's own history; the algorithm is also reimplemented as a modifier in vLLM's llm-compressor.
systems.verification_note: License, method, and calibration approach confirmed from the GitHub README; commit history shows no activity since July 2024. The accuracy/speedup figures are the original ICML 2023 paper's own numbers (vendor-claim).

systems.name: VPTQ (Vector Post-Training Quantization)
systems.method: Vector quantization rather than scalar quantization: groups weights into vectors and quantizes each vector against a learned codebook (lookup table) using second-order (Hessian-based) optimization, refined channel-independently. Dequantization at inference is a simple lookup-table read rather than a per-weight scale/zero-point computation.
systems.availability: Python library / CLI (research release)
systems.best_for: Squeezing very large models (70B-405B) onto far less hardware than scalar 4-bit quantization allows, when the accuracy hit at sub-2-bit is acceptable for the use case.
systems.watch: The README itself carries the caveat: "VPTQ should only be used for research and experimental purposes. Further testing and validation are needed" — treat it as pre-production tooling. That caveat is stronger for the quantization step specifically: the end-to-end quantization driver (`run_vptq.py`) is not in the main branch's pip-installable package — it lives on a separate `algorithm` git branch, itself labeled "an early-release version extracted from a complete experimental codebase" with documented known issues (some parameters like `enable_perm`/`enable_norm` untested, CUDA implementation incomplete for `outlier`/`group_num`), and needs extra RAPIDS/cuml dependencies beyond the base package. The `main`-branch CLI is oriented toward loading and running already-quantized checkpoints, not producing your own. Inference support is CUDA-first, with ROCm support still described as early.
systems.standout: Vector (codebook/lookup-table) quantization is what lets it hold accuracy at 1-2 bits, a range where scalar GPTQ/AWQ-style methods degrade sharply.
systems.calibration: Needs calibration data for its second-order (Hessian-based) optimization; the repo reports roughly 17 hours to quantize a 405B-parameter model end to end.
systems.bit_widths: Sub-2-bit through 4-bit; published configs include 1.375-bit, 1.5-bit, 2-bit, and 3-bit variants
systems.accuracy_note: The VPTQ paper/repo reports better accuracy than other extreme-low-bit methods (e.g. AQLM, QuIP#) at 1-2 bit on published WikiText-2 perplexity tables; these are the team's own reported numbers, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Custom CUDA kernels for lookup-table dequantization; early ROCm support; integration with the Aphrodite inference engine noted in the repo.
systems.output_format: VPTQ checkpoint (codebook + indices), distributed as complete Hugging Face-compatible model repos
systems.adoption: Microsoft Research project, published at EMNLP 2024; pre-quantized checkpoints (7B-405B) published under the VPTQ-community org on Hugging Face.
systems.verification_note: License, method, bit-widths, and the maintainer's own "research and experimental purposes" disclaimer confirmed from the GitHub README; commit history shows no activity since April 2025. The 405B/17-hour figure and comparative accuracy numbers are the team's own reported results (vendor-claim).

systems.name: bitsandbytes
systems.method: On-the-fly, calibration-free weight-only quantization applied at model load time: LLM.int8() does vector-wise 8-bit quantization with a mixed-precision fp16 decomposition for outlier features, and NF4/FP4 do 4-bit quantization using a distribution-aware nonlinear datatype (NF4, from the QLoRA paper). Quantization parameters are derived from block-wise weight statistics (absmax), not from a calibration dataset or an optimization loop.
systems.availability: Python library (deep Hugging Face Transformers/PEFT integration)
systems.best_for: The lowest-friction way to load a model at reduced memory (`load_in_4bit=True`) for QLoRA-style fine-tuning or direct inference from Transformers, with no separate quantization step or exported checkpoint required.
systems.watch: By default, bitsandbytes quantizes weights on the fly at load time rather than as a separate production step, so a model loaded with `load_in_4bit=True`/`load_in_8bit=True` re-quantizes on every load unless you explicitly persist the quantized weights via `save_pretrained()`/`push_to_hub()` — which is common practice (many '-bnb-4bit'/'-bnb-8bit' checkpoints are published this way on the Hugging Face Hub) and skips re-quantization on reload. Even a saved bnb checkpoint is a narrower ecosystem than GPTQ/AWQ: it's tied to the bitsandbytes runtime rather than a vendor-neutral file format, though support now extends beyond Transformers — vLLM auto-detects and loads bnb-quantized checkpoints directly.
systems.standout: The only tool in this category built primarily for QLoRA-style fine-tuning (quantized base weights plus trainable LoRA adapters) rather than a pure inference-serving export.
systems.calibration: Calibration-free — quantization parameters are computed directly from block-wise weight statistics at load time, no dataset or forward passes needed.
systems.bit_widths: 8-bit (LLM.int8()) and 4-bit (NF4 / FP4)
systems.accuracy_note: The original LLM.int8() paper reports no accuracy degradation versus FP16 at 8-bit via its mixed-precision outlier decomposition, and the QLoRA paper reports NF4 4-bit fine-tuning matching 16-bit fine-tuning quality; both are the original authors' own published results, not independently reproduced here.
systems.kernel_support: Its own CUDA kernels are the primary, most mature path; recent releases add multi-backend support (AMD GPU, Intel XPU, Intel Gaudi HPU, CPU, Apple MPS) for inference.
systems.output_format: Not a portable pre-quantized checkpoint by default — the base model stays fp16/bf16 on disk and is quantized on the fly at load time. bitsandbytes can serialize a 4-bit/8-bit quantized checkpoint via `save_pretrained()`/`push_to_hub()` (the basis for the many '-bnb-4bit' repos on the HF Hub), and reloading one skips re-quantization, but it still requires the bitsandbytes runtime to load rather than being a serving-ecosystem-neutral format.
systems.adoption: Sponsored by Hugging Face; the default backend behind Transformers' `load_in_4bit`/`load_in_8bit` and the reference implementation used for QLoRA fine-tuning.
systems.verification_note: License, method, and hardware support confirmed from the GitHub README; the LLM.int8()/QLoRA accuracy claims are the original papers' own reported results (vendor-claim).

systems.name: llm-compressor
systems.method: A modifier-based framework rather than a single algorithm: implements RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, AutoRound, and rotation-based methods (SpinQuant, QuIP) for weight and/or activation quantization, plus structured MoE expert pruning (REAP). You assemble a "recipe" of modifiers, each applied via calibration forward passes over the target model.
systems.availability: Python library / CLI, Transformers-compatible
systems.best_for: Teams standardizing on vLLM for serving who want one tool covering weight-only, weight+activation, FP8, and KV-cache quantization plus MoE pruning, with output guaranteed to load in vLLM.
systems.watch: Its `compressed-tensors` output and fastest kernel paths (int4, W8A8) are pinned to vLLM serving and specific NVIDIA compute-capability floors (Ampere+ for int4, Ada Lovelace/Hopper+ for FP8), so check your target GPU's compute capability before picking a scheme.
systems.standout: The only tool in this category that bundles multiple established algorithms (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, AutoRound, rotation-based methods) behind one recipe API plus structured MoE expert pruning, rather than shipping a single method.
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration dataset for the calibration-based modifiers (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, AutoRound); supports DDP and disk offload so it can compress models larger than a single GPU's VRAM by sharding/offloading during the calibration pass.
systems.bit_widths: W8A8 (int8, fp8), W4A16, W4AFP8, NVFP4/MXFP4/MXFP8 microscale formats, FP8/NVFP4 KV-cache, and arbitrary WNA4/WNA8/WNA16 combinations depending on the chosen modifier
systems.kernel_support: vLLM's Marlin/Machete (int4), CUTLASS FP8, and microscale kernels on NVIDIA GPUs; specific compute-capability thresholds vary by scheme (Ampere+ for int4, Ada Lovelace/Hopper+ for FP8).
systems.output_format: compressed-tensors safetensors checkpoint, loadable directly by vLLM
systems.adoption: Official vLLM project tooling; used to publish many of the pre-quantized models under the vllm-project and RedHat/neuralmagic Hugging Face orgs.
systems.verification_note: License, supported algorithms/formats, and hardware compute-capability requirements confirmed from the GitHub README (3,149+ commits, active issue/PR activity); no unverified accuracy figures were included.

systems.name: ExLlamaV2 quantizer (EXL2)
systems.method: GPTQ-style calibrated post-training quantization: each weight matrix is quantized multiple times at different bit-widths while measuring reconstruction error against calibration data, then a per-layer/per-column mix of bit-widths is chosen to hit a target average bits-per-weight. Reuses ExLlama's act-order remapping trick to keep mixed-precision layers fast.
systems.availability: Python library + CLI conversion script (convert.py); install via pip or from source
systems.best_for: Squeezing a model onto a fixed VRAM budget on a single consumer GPU by choosing an exact average bitrate rather than snapping to a fixed quant level.
systems.watch: As of a README update on 2026-03-04, the project carries a maintainer-added notice: 'This project is archived for now. Development continues on ExLlamaV3.' This is a README note, not GitHub's own repository-archived flag — the GitHub API reports the repo as not archived, and it is not read-only. No commits have landed since that note (as of this writing, ~5 months). Before it, development was still active: the repo added Qwen3/Qwen3MoE support and shipped bug fixes through mid-2025. EXL2 files remain loadable, and going forward the tool is not expected to gain support for architectures released after the freeze.
systems.standout: Was among the first widely-used local quantizers to mix multiple bit-widths within a single linear layer to hit a precise average bitrate, rather than only offering a fixed set of per-tensor quant levels.
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration dataset (a default set is bundled with the conversion script); quantization measures per-matrix error against it, so it is not calibration-free.
systems.bit_widths: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8-bit, mixable per layer to reach any average bitrate in that range (e.g. a 70B model quantized to 2.55 bpw to fit a single 24GB GPU)
systems.kernel_support: Custom CUDA kernels for NVIDIA GPUs only (targets consumer cards such as the RTX 3090/4090); no CPU or Apple Silicon kernel path
systems.output_format: EXL2
systems.adoption: Was the primary backend for TabbyAPI and a common option in text-generation-webui/lollms-webui before development moved to ExLlamaV3
systems.released: 2023 (EXL2 format introduced as part of ExLlamaV2); archived in favor of ExLlamaV3

systems.name: ExLlamaV3 quantizer (EXL3)
systems.method: Trellis/codebook-based quantization derived from QTIP (Cornell RelaxML): weights are mapped into a procedural codebook and packed into tail-biting trellis structures rather than scalar rounding per group, which the project reports holds coherence at lower bitrates than scalar GPTQ/AWQ-style methods. Conversion needs only an input model in Hugging Face format and a target bitrate.
systems.availability: Python library + CLI conversion script (convert.py); prebuilt wheels, PyPI, or build from source (needs PyTorch, flash-attn-2)
systems.best_for: Running large models at very low bits-per-weight (sub-2-bit) on a single consumer GPU while staying coherent, where scalar quantizers degrade badly.
systems.watch: Quantization is GPU-bound and needs PyTorch/flash-attn-2 built for your CUDA version — there is no CPU conversion path — and as an early-preview successor to EXL2 the project itself initially said it 'is not yet a viable replacement' for every EXL2 use case, so check current model/feature coverage before committing a production pipeline to it.
systems.standout: One of three trellis/codebook-based quantizers in this catalog, not the only one -- QTIP (its direct ancestor) and VPTQ's vector-codebook approach are the other two. Per the project's own docs it shares QTIP's tail-biting-trellis/procedural-codebook scheme but diverges in how tensors are regularized and packed, and unlike QTIP and VPTQ (both dormant/frozen), EXL3 remains actively developed and is served in production via TabbyAPI.
systems.calibration: Requires only the source Hugging Face model and a target bitrate to run — no separate calibration dataset to prepare — with conversion taking minutes for small models up to a few hours for 70B+ on a single RTX 4090-class GPU.
systems.bit_widths: Variable, roughly 1 to 8 bits/weight; the project demonstrates coherent output at 1.6 bpw on Llama-3.1-70B and typically benchmarks around 4 bpw
systems.accuracy_note: Project-published perplexity charts show EXL3 competitive with GGUF I-quants across Llama 3.1 8B/70B, Llama 3.2 1B, and Mistral 7B at matched bitrates — this is a vendor (project-author) comparison, not an independent replication.
systems.kernel_support: NVIDIA Tensor Core CUDA kernels; served via TabbyAPI, the project's official recommended backend
systems.output_format: EXL3
systems.released: Early preview, 2024/2025; actively releasing through 2026 (v1.4.0 shipped August 2026)
systems.verification_note: Accuracy comparisons against GGUF/QTIP are sourced from the project's own README/docs, not an independent benchmark.

systems.name: MLC-LLM quantization (convert_weight)
systems.method: Data-free grouped round-to-nearest weight quantization (qAfB naming: A=weight bits, B=activation bits, e.g. q3f16_1, q4f16_1) compiled ahead-of-time into a hardware-specific kernel library via Apache TVM, rather than producing a generic weight file a runtime interprets at load time. A separate FP8 weight-activation mode (CUDA only) is calibration-based, requiring a max-calibration compile pass over a dataset like ShareGPT before the final quantized build.
systems.availability: Python library + CLI (mlc_llm convert_weight), requires the TVM-based MLC compiler backend
systems.best_for: Deploying a quantized model across MLC-LLM's unusually wide target range (NVIDIA/AMD/Apple GPUs, iOS, Android, and WebGPU browsers) from one compilation pipeline.
systems.watch: A November 2025 GitHub issue (#3382) asking whether the project was abandoned was closed within five days after TVM/MLC project lead Tianqi Chen replied directly: "we are continuing supporting and maintaining the project," noting recent effort has concentrated on low-level compilation/ABI infrastructure (e.g. xgrammar integration, WebGPU support) rather than user-facing features — CPU-offload and structured-output support were still absent at the time. Commit activity has continued since, with pushes into the current month. Architecture coverage has since caught up for some of the models cited in that issue: Qwen3, Qwen3-MoE and Gemma 3 now each have dedicated model directories in the repo. Granite 4 does not, and is still unsupported as of this writing — check your target architecture before depending on it.
systems.standout: Compiles the quantized model into an ahead-of-time, hardware-specific kernel library (via TVM) rather than shipping a generic quantized weight file that a runtime interprets at load time — the same pipeline also targets WebGPU browsers and mobile, which none of the other tools here do.
systems.calibration: Weight-only modes (q3f16_1, q4f16_1, q4f32_1, q0f16/q0f32) are calibration-free grouped RTN; the FP8 weight-activation mode is calibration-based and needs a max-calibrate compile pass over a dataset such as ShareGPT before finalizing.
systems.bit_widths: 0 (unquantized f16/f32 passthrough), 3-bit and 4-bit weight-only group quantization (q3f16_1/q4f16_1/q4f32_1), an experimental 4-bit AWQ mode flagged unstable by the docs, and FP8 (e4m3/e5m2) weight-activation on CUDA
systems.kernel_support: TVM-compiled kernels targeting NVIDIA/AMD/Apple GPUs, iOS, Android, and WebGPU (browser); the compiled library is hardware-specific, unlike a portable weight file
systems.output_format: MLC compiled weight/library bundle (mlc-chat-config.json, tensor-cache.json, sharded params, plus a compiled model library)
systems.adoption: Sibling WebLLM project (same org) remains active for in-browser inference; community discussion cites MLC-LLM as the only engine offering GPU parallelism for multi-user serving across this many device types, though adoption relative to llama.cpp/vLLM is smaller
systems.verification_note: Maintenance status is vendor-confirmed, not merely inferred: MLC/TVM lead Tianqi Chen responded directly in GitHub issue #3382 (closed Nov 2025, 5 days after opening) affirming the project remains actively maintained, and this is corroborated by continuous commit activity into the current month on both mlc-llm and its sibling web-llm repo. The adoption comparison against llama.cpp/vLLM, by contrast, is drawn from informal community discussion rather than any measured figure and should be read as anecdotal, not verified.

systems.name: MLX quantization (mlx-lm)
systems.method: Affine (group-wise scale/zero-point) weight-only quantization by default (mlx_lm.convert -q), plus MXFP4/MXFP8/NVFP4 microscaling modes. A separate DWQ ('distillation with quantization') mode runs gradient descent on the scales/biases of an already-quantized model to minimize output divergence against a full-precision teacher — effectively a lightweight calibration pass rather than full retraining.
systems.availability: Python library + CLI (mlx_lm.convert, mlx_lm.dwq); pip install
systems.best_for: Producing quantized checkpoints tuned to Apple Silicon's unified-memory architecture for on-device Mac inference.
systems.watch: MLX quantized weights only run inside the MLX runtime on Apple Silicon — there's no CUDA or generic-CPU kernel for the format, so a model quantized here can't be redeployed to a Linux GPU box without re-quantizing from the original weights with a different tool.
systems.standout: The only quantizer here whose kernels are co-designed with Apple's own unified-memory GPU path via the MLX framework itself, so quantized MLX models keep the M-series memory-bandwidth advantage that GGUF or EXL2 running under emulation don't target.
systems.calibration: Default affine quantization is calibration-free (round-to-nearest per group); DWQ is a calibration-style refinement that needs a full-precision teacher copy of the model and a training-style pass, and the project notes it works best distilling to 2-4 bit, with 6-8 bit distillation often not helping.
systems.bit_widths: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8-bit affine, plus MXFP4/MXFP8/NVFP4 microscaling modes; configurable group size (e.g. group size 32 for higher-precision targets)
systems.kernel_support: Apple Silicon GPU/unified-memory kernels via the MLX framework only; no NVIDIA/AMD or non-Apple CPU path
systems.output_format: MLX quantized weight format (mlx_model, safetensors-based)
systems.adoption: The mlx-community organization on Hugging Face hosts 5,400+ pre-quantized MLX models (live count, August 2026), covering LLMs, VLMs, audio and image models.
systems.released: MLX framework released by Apple in December 2023; mlx-lm quantization tooling has shipped and expanded continuously since

systems.name: bitnet.cpp
systems.method: Not a post-training quantizer in the GPTQ/AWQ sense: it converts and packs a checkpoint whose ternary {-1,0,+1} weights already exist from quantization-aware pretraining (absmean weight scaling, per-token absmax 8-bit activations — W1.58A8) into optimized GGUF-based kernel layouts (I2_S, and lookup-table-based TL1/TL2 derived from T-MAC) for fast CPU inference.
systems.availability: CLI tool, built from source via CMake (setup_env.py orchestrates model download/conversion/kernel codegen); Python >=3.10, CMake >=3.22, Clang >=18 required to build
systems.best_for: Running Microsoft's native 1.58-bit BitNet model family at genuine ternary precision with fast CPU-only kernels, no GPU required.
systems.watch: You cannot feed bitnet.cpp an arbitrary fp16/bf16 checkpoint and get a 1.58-bit model out — the ternary weights must already exist from quantization-aware pretraining; the tool only converts and kernel-packs models that were trained ternary from the start (e.g. Microsoft's own bitnet-b1.58 releases), so it is not a general-purpose quantizer for existing dense models.
systems.standout: The only tool in this category that isn't really doing post-training quantization at all — it packs weights that are already ternary from training, which is how it reaches genuine 1.58-bit weights without the accuracy hit a PTQ pass to that bit-width would normally cause.
systems.calibration: No calibration dataset needed for the conversion/packing step itself — the ternary weights come from QAT during pretraining, so setup_env.py is a deterministic format conversion, not a data-driven calibration pass.
systems.bit_widths: 1.58-bit ternary weights ({-1,0,+1}, absmean-scaled) with 8-bit per-token activations (W1.58A8)
systems.kernel_support: Optimized CPU kernels for ARM (NEON) and x86 (AVX2); project reports 1.37x-5.07x ARM speedups and 2.37x-6.17x x86 speedups over baseline with substantial energy reduction; GPU kernels available, NPU support described as upcoming
systems.output_format: GGUF (BitNet-specific I2_S / TL1 / TL2 kernel layouts, e.g. ggml-model-i2_s.gguf)
systems.adoption: Official inference framework for Microsoft's bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T model family on Hugging Face; adoption is limited to models specifically trained ternary, which is a small but growing set
systems.released: Bitnet.cpp 1.0 (CPU inference) announced October 17, 2024; official BitNet-b1.58-2B-4T model released April 14, 2025; GPU inference kernel added May 20, 2025; active ongoing releases continuing through at least July 2026 (BitNet embedding models, VibeASR.cpp).
systems.verification_note: Licence, conversion/packing mechanics, and 1.58-bit ternary format confirmed directly against the tool's own README. The ARM (1.37x-5.07x) and x86 (2.37x-6.17x) inference speedup figures in kernel_support are the project's own reported benchmarks, not independently reproduced here -- hence verification: mixed rather than verified.

systems.name: coremltools (Apple)
systems.method: Two families, both via the coremltools.optimize API: (1) linear/affine PTQ of weights (8-bit or 4-bit, per-tensor/per-channel/per-block) via round-to-nearest (data-free) or a GPTQ-style layer-wise calibrated algorithm (~128 samples), plus optional 8-bit activation quantization (needs calibration data to observe activation ranges); and (2) palettization, which replaces weights with shared-codebook lookup-table indices at 1-8 bits. A separate coremltools.optimize.torch API adds quantization-aware training/fine-tuning for accuracy recovery before export.
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install coremltools`, plus coremltools.optimize.torch for the PyTorch-side calibrated/QAT paths); converts and compresses PyTorch/TensorFlow models into Core ML .mlpackage files
systems.best_for: Compressing a PyTorch/TensorFlow model for on-device deployment on iOS/macOS/visionOS, specifically to exploit the Apple Neural Engine rather than just GPU or CPU.
systems.watch: The output format (.mlpackage) only runs via the Core ML runtime on Apple devices -- this is not a portable checkpoint for llama.cpp/vLLM/TensorRT-style serving, it is an Apple-platform-only endpoint. The best-quality calibrated path (GPTQ-style LayerwiseCompressor) also only runs against the PyTorch model before Core ML conversion via coremltools.optimize.torch, not on the exported .mlpackage -- post-export, only the data-free coremltools.optimize.coreml linear/palettization path is available, so which API you use depends on which stage of the pipeline you're at. coremltools also ships wheels only for macOS (10.13+) and Linux (manylinux1 x86-64) -- there is no official Windows wheel, despite PyTorch/TensorFlow themselves supporting Windows.
systems.standout: The only quantizer here that targets Apple's Neural Engine specifically (not just GPU/CPU) via palettization lookup tables the Neural Engine executes natively, palettizes down to 1 bit per weight as a first-class API (not just rounding), and is the only one offering an official quantization-aware training path rather than post-training-only.
systems.calibration: Data-free for standard linear weight quantization and palettization (RTN); calibration data required for activation quantization and the GPTQ-style LayerwiseCompressor -- Apple's own docs state around 128 samples are usually sufficient to build per-layer Hessian statistics.
systems.bit_widths: Linear quantization: 8-bit and 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations. Palettization: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8-bit lookup-table indices.
systems.accuracy_note: Apple's own guide reports ResNet50 weight-only PTQ at 76.10% top-1 vs. a 76.14% Float16 baseline, and QAT recovering to 76.80% +/- 0.05% -- vendor-reported, not independently confirmed here.
systems.kernel_support: Apple Neural Engine, GPU, and CPU on iOS/iPadOS/macOS/visionOS via the Core ML runtime; palettization is called out as working best on the Neural Engine, while linear quantization shows more benefit on GPU.
systems.output_format: Core ML model package (.mlpackage)
systems.adoption: Apple's official model-conversion/compression toolkit for Core ML; used broadly across the iOS/macOS app ecosystem for on-device model deployment.
systems.released: coremltools has shipped since 2017; the coremltools.optimize compression APIs (palettization, calibrated quantization, QAT) shipped in coremltools 7 (2023).
systems.verification_note: Method, bit-width, and licence details confirmed via the official apple.github.io/coremltools docs and GitHub LICENSE; the ResNet50 accuracy comparison is Apple's own published figure, not independently reproduced.

systems.name: llama.cpp quantize (GGUF)
systems.price_note: Free, open source (MIT); no paid tier
systems.method: Post-training, weight-only quantization of a GGUF/BF16 model. Round-to-nearest by default; accuracy is improved with an optional 'importance matrix' (imatrix) computed by a separate `llama-imatrix` pass over a calibration text file, which weights the rounding by observed per-weight activation magnitude. K-quants use block-wise scalar quantization with mixed internal precision per block; I-quants add a shared-codebook (non-uniform) scheme for the lowest bit-widths. `--tensor-type` allows per-tensor/per-layer regex overrides, including different precision for MoE routed vs. shared experts.
systems.availability: CLI tool (`llama-quantize`, built from source or via prebuilt release binaries); wrapped by third-party front-ends like the GGUF-my-repo Hugging Face Space
systems.best_for: Producing CPU-and-GPU-portable GGUF checkpoints for llama.cpp and its downstream runtimes (Ollama, LM Studio, koboldcpp, text-generation-webui, jan).
systems.watch: Round-to-nearest K-quants run with zero calibration data, but the low-bit I-quants and the best K-quant results both depend on a separate imatrix pass most casual users skip — running quantize straight off the base GGUF gives measurably worse low-bit accuracy than the same Q-level from an imatrix-calibrated build (e.g. the ones bartowski/unsloth publish).
systems.standout: The only quantizer here whose output runs with zero GPU at inference time, on nearly any CPU architecture, which is what made GGUF the default format for local, CPU-friendly serving.
systems.calibration: Calibration-free by default (round-to-nearest); an optional llama-imatrix pass over a plain-text calibration corpus (commonly ~30k-token Wikitext-style samples) measurably improves accuracy, especially for I-quants and sub-4-bit K-quants. imatrix generation time scales with model size and calibration corpus length.
systems.bit_widths: ~2 to 8.5 bits/weight nominal: K-quants (Q2_K-Q8_0, block-wise with per-block scale/min) and I-quants (IQ1_S/IQ1_M through IQ4_XS/IQ4_NL, shared-codebook, aimed at the low-bit end)
systems.accuracy_note: Community perplexity comparisons on 7B-class models put Q4_K_M about 0.05 perplexity points above F16 (original k-quants benchmark: ~5.96 vs ~5.91) and Q8_0 within ~0.0004; the gap widens sharply below 3 bits, which is why I-quants and imatrix exist.
systems.kernel_support: Optimized ggml kernels for x86 (AVX/AVX2/AVX-512), ARM (NEON), Apple Silicon (Metal), and CUDA/ROCm/Vulkan GPU offload — the broadest inference hardware coverage of any format in this list
systems.output_format: GGUF
systems.adoption: GGUF is the most widely distributed quantized-weight format on Hugging Face; prolific community quantizers (bartowski, unsloth, mradermacher) publish imatrix-calibrated GGUF repos for nearly every notable open release
systems.released: quantize tool shipped with llama.cpp's initial 2023 release; K-quants added mid-2023 (PR #1684, merged June 2023); I-quants added in early 2024, not late 2023 (IQ2_XXS, PR #4773, merged January 2024)
systems.verification_note: Licence, K-quant/I-quant/imatrix mechanics, and the MoE routed-vs-shared-expert --tensor-type override confirmed directly against the tool's own README. Of accuracy_note's two perplexity figures, only Q4_K_M was independently checked against PR #1684 (the original K-quants PR)'s own perplexity table -- a primary, inspectable source, not a vendor claim -- which is also where an initial wrong Q4_K_M figure was corrected. The Q8_0 figure is a widely-repeated community number (reproduced in llama.cpp's historical README and downstream sources) that was not pinned to one specific primary source, hence verification: mixed rather than verified for the row as a whole. The hardware and released-date figures were separately corrected against published GGUF file sizes and GitHub's PR merge history.

systems.name: AMD Quark
systems.method: Post-training quantization (a 'fake quantization' simulate-then-convert workflow) plus FX Graph Mode PTQ and quantization-aware training, for PyTorch and ONNX models; calibration is done through configurable observers (per-tensor/per-channel MinMax, percentile, or per-block MX observers) that need a representative dataset run through the model to compute scales and zero-points
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install amd-quark`) with separate PyTorch and ONNX APIs
systems.best_for: Producing one quantized PyTorch/ONNX checkpoint for AMD's own inference stack -- Ryzen AI NPUs via ONNX Runtime's Vitis AI execution provider, or Instinct GPUs via ROCm -- with ONNX QDQ and JSON-safetensors as the general-purpose export targets; GGUF export is available only for int4 group-32 quantization on four specific Llama architectures, not as a general format choice.
systems.watch: Quantization runs on Linux with CPU or GPU acceleration; Windows is supported but CPU-only, so calibrating a large model on a Windows workstation has no GPU acceleration path
systems.standout: Exports one PyTorch quantization run to both ONNX QDQ and JSON-safetensors for general deployment; GGUF export also exists but only for one specific configuration (asymmetric int4 per-group, group_size=32, i.e. GGUF's Q4_1 type) on four supported architectures (Llama2-7B/13B/70B, Llama3-8B) -- not a general GGUF path.
systems.calibration: Needs calibration data passed through configurable observers (MinMax/percentile/MX); no calibration-free default is documented
systems.bit_widths: 16-bit down to 4-bit integer and floating-point (int4/int8/int16, fp4/fp8/fp16/bf16), plus block-floating-point MX formats
systems.kernel_support: AMD Ryzen AI NPUs via ONNX Runtime's Vitis AI Execution Provider (auto-partitions NPU/CPU subgraphs), and ROCm GPUs for PyTorch-format output. Quark also integrates with AMD Pytorch-light (APL) for INT-K/BFP16/BRECQ schemes, but APL is AMD's internal framework -- external users must separately request access; it is not part of the open-source pip package.
systems.output_format: ONNX (QDQ) and JSON-safetensors for any supported quantized model; GGUF is also supported but limited to asymmetric int4 per-group (group_size=32) quantization on Llama2-7B/13B/70B and Llama3-8B only.
systems.verification_note: Confirmed via the official quark.docs.amd.com documentation and the amd/quark GitHub LICENSE file.

systems.name: Intel Neural Compressor
systems.method: Broad PTQ/QAT toolkit spanning static and dynamic INT8 quantization, SmoothQuant (pre-quantization activation smoothing), weight-only quantization (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, TEQ) for LLMs, and integration with AutoRound -- Intel's own sign-gradient-descent rounding algorithm -- for accurate INT4/INT3/INT2 and MXFP4/NVFP4; static/SmoothQuant/AutoRound paths need a representative calibration dataset, weight-only RTN is calibration-free
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install neural-compressor`), CLI utilities; also used as a backend inside Hugging Face Optimum, Microsoft Olive, and PyTorch/TensorFlow/ONNX Runtime
systems.best_for: Getting INT8/INT4 (or lower, via AutoRound) checkpoints tuned for Intel Xeon (AMX/VNNI), Gaudi accelerators, and Core Ultra NPUs directly out of the PyTorch/TensorFlow/ONNX models you already train
systems.watch: Intel states 'extensive testing' only for Intel hardware (Gaudi, Xeon, Core Ultra, Data Center GPU); AMD CPU, Arm CPU, and Nvidia GPU are explicitly listed as 'limited testing' only, so validation on non-Intel silicon is thinner than the hardware list suggests
systems.standout: The widest single-library algorithm menu in this category (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ/TEQ/SmoothQuant/AutoRound/QAT/mixed-precision) spanning PyTorch, TensorFlow, and ONNX Runtime rather than being tied to one framework
systems.calibration: Static/SmoothQuant/AutoRound paths need a calibration dataset (typically a few hundred samples); weight-only RTN is calibration-free
systems.bit_widths: INT8, INT4, INT3, INT2 (via AutoRound), FP8, MXFP8, MXFP4, NVFP4
systems.kernel_support: Intel Xeon (AMX/VNNI), Intel Gaudi, Intel Core Ultra NPU, Intel Data Center GPU Max/Flex; also runs (limited testing) via PyTorch/ONNX Runtime on AMD CPU, Arm CPU, and Nvidia GPU
systems.output_format: Hugging Face safetensors checkpoint, plus ONNX and TensorFlow SavedModel depending on the source framework
systems.released: First released 2021 (as Intel Low Precision Optimization Tool, later renamed Neural Compressor); current major version 3.x
systems.verification_note: Confirmed via the official GitHub README, docs.intel.github.io quantization guide, and the intel/auto-round repo README for bit-width claims.

systems.name: Intel OpenVINO NNCF
systems.method: Post-training quantization and quantization-aware training. Default 8-bit PTQ gathers activation statistics from a small calibration set (~300 samples, asymmetric INT8 by default); a separate LLM 'weight compression' path (`nncf.compress_weights`) can run calibration-free (data-free RTN to INT4/INT8) or with an optional AWQ/scale-estimation refinement pass that does use calibration data for better INT4 accuracy
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install nncf`); also the compression backend built into the OpenVINO toolkit and Hugging Face Optimum-Intel
systems.best_for: Compressing PyTorch/TensorFlow/ONNX models specifically for OpenVINO's own Intel CPU/iGPU/NPU runtime, especially INT4 weight compression for LLMs running on Intel AI-PC laptops
systems.watch: NNCF's fastest and most common paths (8-bit PTQ, or INT4 weight compression without AWQ) are Intel-runtime-specific by design -- the output is most useful once converted to OpenVINO IR, so using it purely as a generic PyTorch/ONNX quantizer for non-Intel deployment is a secondary use case
systems.standout: Offers a genuinely calibration-free INT4 weight-compression path for LLMs (data-free RTN) in the same API as a calibrated AWQ path, letting you skip calibration entirely when no representative data is available
systems.calibration: 8-bit PTQ needs roughly 300 calibration samples; INT4 LLM weight compression can run calibration-free (data-free) or with an optional calibrated AWQ/scale-estimation refinement
systems.bit_widths: INT8 (weights + activations), INT4 weight-only for LLMs
systems.kernel_support: OpenVINO runtime on Intel CPU, integrated/discrete GPU, and NPU
systems.output_format: OpenVINO IR (.xml/.bin); also ONNX and PyTorch state-dict export
systems.released: First released around 2020 (NNCF arXiv paper published February 2020); developed continuously as part of the OpenVINO toolkit
systems.verification_note: Confirmed via the official openvinotoolkit/nncf GitHub repo and OpenVINO documentation.

systems.name: Microsoft Olive
systems.method: An orchestration framework rather than a single algorithm: wires together other vendors' quantizers as interchangeable 'passes' -- AutoGPTQ (weight-only GPTQ at 8/4/3/2-bit), AutoAWQ (4-bit AWQ), RTN and HQQ (both calibration-free), ONNX Runtime static/dynamic quantization, plus pass-through integrations for Intel Neural Compressor, AMD Quark, NVIDIA ModelOpt (AWQ/RTN), and Qualcomm AIMET (LPBQ/SeqMSE/AdaRound); also offers QuaRot/SpinQuant weight-rotation as a pre-quantization accuracy-improving step
systems.availability: Python CLI + library (`pip install olive-ai`), config-driven (YAML/JSON) pipelines
systems.best_for: Teams targeting ONNX Runtime across heterogeneous hardware (CPU/GPU/NPU) who want one CLI to try several quantization backends against the same model without hand-integrating each library
systems.watch: Olive itself implements very little quantization math directly -- accuracy and calibration behavior are inherited entirely from whichever underlying pass you select (GPTQ vs AWQ vs RTN, etc.), so evaluating 'Olive's' output quality really means evaluating the wrapped library's algorithm
systems.standout: The only tool here explicitly designed to be hardware- and algorithm-agnostic -- one config can swap between GPTQ, AWQ, RTN, HQQ, Neural Compressor, or Quark backends and always land on a single ONNX output
systems.calibration: Depends on the selected pass -- RTN and HQQ are calibration-free; static ONNX Runtime quantization and GPTQ/AWQ need a calibration dataset
systems.bit_widths: 2 to 8-bit, depending on the wrapped algorithm (down to 2-bit via the AutoGPTQ pass)
systems.kernel_support: ONNX Runtime execution providers -- CPU, CUDA/TensorRT, DirectML, OpenVINO, and QNN (Qualcomm NPU)
systems.output_format: ONNX
systems.released: Initial public release 2023 (announced at Microsoft Build 2023; PyPI package olive-ai first published March 2023); actively developed through 2026
systems.verification_note: Confirmed via the official microsoft.github.io/Olive quantization docs and the microsoft/Olive GitHub repo (MIT LICENSE file).

systems.name: NVIDIA Model Optimizer (ModelOpt, formerly TensorRT Model Optimizer)
systems.price_note: Free, open source (Apache-2.0); the checkpoints it produces are meant for NVIDIA's own inference stack, which is itself free to self-host
systems.method: Post-training quantization via AWQ (activation-aware weight-only INT4), plain RTN-equivalent max-calibration, and calibrated FP8/NVFP4 conversion, plus quantization-aware training (QAT); calibration runs a small set of representative prompts (commonly 32-512 samples, e.g. `--calib_size 32`) through the full-precision model to collect activation statistics before compressing weights (and optionally activations) to FP8, INT4, INT8, or NVFP4. NVFP4 quantization can also be scoped to mixture-of-experts layers only (`nvfp4_experts_only`, matching `*mlp.experts*`/`*block_sparse_moe*`) for MoE models.
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install nvidia-modelopt`) with CLI example scripts, also shipped as an NVIDIA NGC container
systems.best_for: Teams already deploying on TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, or SGLang who want FP8 or NVFP4 checkpoints tuned specifically for Nvidia's own Hopper/Blackwell inference kernels
systems.watch: The quantization step itself needs an NVIDIA GPU (calibration runs the fp16/bf16 model forward), and a 70B+ model can OOM without `--use_seq_device_map` or `--low_memory_mode`; NVFP4's hardware speedup is Blackwell-specific, so the format quantizes fine on older Ampere/Hopper cards but won't accelerate there
systems.standout: The only tool here shipping NVFP4 (Nvidia's Blackwell-native 4-bit microscaling format) alongside a unified Hugging Face checkpoint exporter that round-trips into TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang from a single export call
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration set (commonly 32-512 prompts) run through the model to collect activation statistics; weight-only RTN paths need less data than AWQ/FP8 activation calibration
systems.bit_widths: FP8, INT8, INT4 (AWQ), NVFP4 (4-bit microscaling)
systems.kernel_support: TensorRT-LLM, TensorRT, vLLM, and SGLang; NVFP4 acceleration requires Blackwell-class GPUs
systems.output_format: Unified Hugging Face checkpoint (safetensors) via ModelOpt's export API; also TensorRT-LLM-specific checkpoint export
systems.adoption: Used by NVIDIA itself to publish pre-quantized FP8/NVFP4 checkpoints of Llama, DeepSeek-R1, and other open-weight releases on Hugging Face
systems.released: Open-sourced January 2025 (long-standing internal tool before that); officially rebranded from 'NVIDIA TensorRT Model Optimizer' to 'NVIDIA Model Optimizer' in December 2025; actively released through 2026 (a 0.46.0 release candidate shipped within the past week of this review).
systems.verification_note: Method, formats, licence, hardware behavior, MoE-scoped quantization, and current project naming confirmed against the live GitHub repo (NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer, formerly NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer, rebranded per its own changelog on 2025-12-08), its config.py source, the hf_ptq example README, GitHub API metadata (license field, push/release timestamps), and Hugging Face listings for NVIDIA's own published NVFP4/FP4 checkpoints (e.g. DeepSeek-R1-NVFP4, DeepSeek-V3.1-NVFP4); no independently-verified accuracy/perplexity figure is included.

systems.name: Qualcomm AIMET (AI Model Efficiency Toolkit)
systems.method: Post-training quantization pipeline combining BatchNorm folding and Cross-Layer Equalization (both data-free), 'Calibration'/QuantSim range-setting, AdaRound weight rounding, SeqMSE per-layer optimization, and AutoQuant to auto-search a recipe that hits a target accuracy; also supports quantization-aware training via aimet-torch
systems.availability: Python packages aimet-torch and aimet-onnx, open source, released roughly every 2 weeks on PyPI (current AIMET/v2 supports only PyTorch and ONNX per the official README). A separate aimet-tensorflow PyPI listing exists but has shipped exactly one placeholder release ('Coming soon!', v0.0.1, Feb 2024) and is not part of the current, actively-maintained toolkit — TensorFlow was supported only in the legacy 1.x line.
systems.best_for: Preparing PyTorch/ONNX models for deployment on Qualcomm Snapdragon/Hexagon NPUs via SNPE or the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct (QNN) stack
systems.watch: AIMET's core PTQ recipes (AdaRound, QuantSim range-setting, SeqMSE) need calibration data, so despite the data-free CLE/BN-folding stage, it is not the calibration-free option in this category overall
systems.standout: AutoQuant automatically searches and applies the right combination of AIMET's own techniques (CLE, BN-folding, AdaRound) to hit a target accuracy, rather than requiring you to hand-pick a quantization recipe
systems.calibration: Needs a calibration dataset for AdaRound/QuantSim range-setting/SeqMSE; BatchNorm folding and Cross-Layer Equalization stages are data-free
systems.bit_widths: INT8 down to INT4 (e.g. INT4-weights/INT8-activations configurations are documented)
systems.accuracy_note: Qualcomm reports ResNet-50 losing under 0.9% top-1 accuracy all the way down to 8-bit quantization -- vendor-reported, not independently confirmed
systems.kernel_support: Qualcomm Hexagon DSP/NPU via SNPE and QNN; Qualcomm reports 5-15x speedup there over the Kryo CPU for INT8 models
systems.output_format: Quantized PyTorch or ONNX checkpoints (QuantSim-annotated), exported onward to SNPE/QNN for Qualcomm silicon
systems.released: Open-sourced May 2020; actively releasing through 2026 (v2.36.0, released July 29, 2026; AIMET ships roughly every 2 weeks on PyPI, so check pypi.org/project/aimet-torch for the current figure)
systems.verification_note: Method, licence, and hardware targets confirmed via the official qualcomm/aimet GitHub repo and Qualcomm developer docs; the ResNet-50 accuracy figure is Qualcomm's own reported number.

systems.name: Unsloth Dynamic quantization
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (core quantization/training code); optional Unsloth Studio UI is AGPL-3.0
systems.price_note: Free, open source; pre-built GGUFs are published free on Hugging Face
systems.method: Post-training quantization producing GGUF files: a per-layer 'Dynamic 2.0' sensitivity search assigns a different GGUF quant type to every layer/tensor (from 1-bit up to 8-bit) instead of applying one uniform scheme, calibrated against Unsloth's own curated 300K-1.5M token chat dataset rather than a user-supplied calibration set or the stock llama.cpp importance matrix; weight-only quantization
systems.availability: Python library (`pip install unsloth`) plus pre-built GGUF files published on Hugging Face; the actual bit-packing is done via llama.cpp's quantize tool under the hood
systems.best_for: Squeezing large open-weight models -- including MoE models like Llama 4 and DeepSeek -- down to run on consumer GPUs/CPUs via llama.cpp-family runtimes, when accuracy at very low bit-widths matters more than a fully generic pipeline
systems.watch: The per-layer scheme is retuned per model release rather than being a general-purpose algorithm you point at an arbitrary checkpoint the way AWQ/GPTQ are -- it ships as pre-built GGUFs for the specific models Unsloth chooses to cover
systems.standout: Claims to beat both the standard llama.cpp importance-matrix (imatrix) quantization and full QAT checkpoints on KL-divergence/MMLU at matched bit-width -- the only tool in this category making that specific head-to-head comparison
systems.calibration: Uses a built-in curated calibration dataset (300K-1.5M tokens depending on model), not user-supplied; the conversion step supports CPU-only operation as well as GPU
systems.bit_widths: 1-bit through 8-bit GGUF quant types (IQ1_S/IQ1_M up to Q8_0), mixed per layer within one model
systems.accuracy_note: The often-cited 67.07% vs 67.15% Gemma 3 12B 5-shot MMLU figure is Google's own, not Unsloth's Dynamic 2.0 output -- it is Google's quantization-aware-trained (QAT) Q4_0 checkpoint versus its bf16 baseline, which Unsloth independently replicated and benchmarked. Unsloth's own claim for Dynamic 2.0 itself is lower KL-divergence than standard imatrix and QAT quants across Llama 4/Gemma 3/Qwen3.5 -- both vendor-reported, not independently reproduced here
systems.kernel_support: llama.cpp and any llama.cpp-based runtime (Ollama, LM Studio, koboldcpp, Open WebUI)
systems.output_format: GGUF
systems.released: Dynamic 2.0 announced 2025; Unsloth's original (MoE-only) Dynamic quantization predates it
systems.verification_note: Method and format confirmed via Unsloth's official docs and blog; the KL-divergence comparison is Unsloth's own Dynamic 2.0 benchmark, not independently reproduced. The Gemma 3 12B MMLU figure (67.07% vs 67.15%) is Google's own QAT-checkpoint benchmark, which Unsloth's blog post replicates and reports -- it is not a Dynamic 2.0 output, and the accuracy_note has been corrected to attribute it correctly (see corrections).

corrections.claim: AutoRound Kernel (ARK) ships flash-attention kernels for Intel CPU/XPU (kernel_support, AutoRound row).
corrections.reality: ARK's own README names its accelerated attention path as SageAttention -- INT8-quantized SDPA variants (sagev1, sagev1_pvi8, sage_dynquant) for Intel Arc GPUs. "Flash attention" appears only as a label for ARK's standard FP16/BF16 SDPA kernel, not as the differentiating technique. kernel_support has been corrected to name SageAttention.

corrections.claim: ExLlamaV3 (EXL3) is "the only tool here using a trellis/codebook quantizer instead of scalar or group-wise rounding" (standout, ExLlamaV3 row).
corrections.reality: QTIP and VPTQ, both cataloged on this same page, are also trellis/vector-codebook methods, and EXL3's own method field already states it is derived from QTIP -- so EXL3 is one of three such quantizers here, not the only one. The standout field has been corrected to name what actually distinguishes it: unlike QTIP and VPTQ (both dormant/frozen), EXL3 remains actively developed and served in production via TabbyAPI, and per the project's own docs it diverges from its QTIP ancestor in how tensors are regularized and packed.

corrections.claim: MLX's kernels are co-designed with Apple's own unified-memory GPU/Neural Engine path (standout, MLX quantization row).
corrections.reality: MLX does not use the Apple Neural Engine at all. The project's own README states device support is "currently the CPU and GPU," and a maintainer closed the repo's ANE-support request (ml-explore/mlx#18) citing the Neural Engine's closed-source API. The standout field has been corrected to describe only MLX's unified-memory GPU kernel co-design, matching this row's own kernel_support field.

corrections.claim: Unsloth's Dynamic quantization scores 67.07% on 5-shot MMLU for Gemma 3 12B versus 67.15% for the full bf16 model (accuracy_note, Unsloth row).
corrections.reality: That comparison is Google's own: Unsloth's blog post reports 67.07% for Google's quantization-aware-trained (QAT) Q4_0 checkpoint of Gemma 3 12B against the bf16 baseline, which Unsloth independently replicated and benchmarked -- it is not output from Unsloth's own Dynamic 2.0 algorithm. The accuracy_note has been corrected to attribute the figure to Google's QAT checkpoint and to state separately what Unsloth claims for Dynamic 2.0 itself (lower KL-divergence than standard imatrix and QAT quants).

gaps: coremltools (Apple's Core ML quantization/palettization toolkit) was independently researched under both format-native and vendor-toolchain -- it genuinely straddles both (a vendor-shipped toolkit that also produces one specific ecosystem's own format) -- and the two research passes were merged into a single format-native row rather than published as two disagreeing entries under slightly different names.

This catalog does not attempt to be exhaustive -- it covers 23 tools found through a structured research pass across three categories (9 generic-algorithm, 7 format-native, 7 vendor-toolchain after the coremltools merge), not every quantization tool that exists. Runtimes' own quant-specialist rows (ExLlamaV3, GPTQModel, bitnet.cpp, VPTQ, QTIP) were each researched fresh here through this page's own production-focused questions rather than copied from that page. AutoGPTQ was not researched as its own row -- GPTQModel's own row documents it as AutoGPTQ's direct successor and fork, per the project's own history ("fully supplanted AutoGPTQ and AutoAWQ" for Hugging Face integration), so a separate AutoGPTQ row would have described a project whose own maintained continuation is already covered. QServe/OmniServe was judged, after research, to be primarily a serving system with no separable quantization-production story of its own distinct from the generic algorithms it applies, and was left off this page rather than forced in.

The `hardware` field (what it takes to run the quantization step itself) is populated only where a row's own research established a genuine CPU-only path; every GPU-requiring row left it absent rather than guessing a specific VRAM tier no source actually stated -- the `calibration` and `method` fields carry the fuller hardware-need description in prose for those rows.

The `edge-capable` and `browser` facets do not apply to any row on this page: every quantization tool needs a real CPU/GPU workstation to run the quantization step, even the ones (bitnet.cpp, AMD Quark, Intel OpenVINO NNCF, Microsoft Olive, Qualcomm AIMET, MLC-LLM) whose OUTPUT is meant to run on a phone/NPU/browser/edge device. That distinction -- what the tool needs vs. what the tool produces for -- is exactly what `hardware` on this page is scoped to, and it is captured in prose in each row's `best_for`/`method` fields instead.
